title: What is caching in Spark — keeping computed partitions available on executors for reuse to avoid recomputation — and why is `cache()` lazy (no computation happens until an action triggers it)?
shortTitle: Caching in Spark and why cache() is lazy

s1_definition.profdef: Caching in Spark keeps the computed partitions of an RDD or DataFrame in executor memory, and optionally on disk, so that subsequent actions reuse them instead of recomputing the whole lineage. The `cache()` method is lazy: calling it only marks the dataset to be cached and registers the intent with the storage system, but no computation and no storage happens until an action triggers execution, at which point the partitions are both computed and stored, and later actions read from the cache.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India spends an hour assembling a complicated summary of Rajesh's year of transactions. If every later question about that summary made him redo the whole hour of work, it would be madness. Caching is keeping that finished summary on his desk so the next ten questions are answered instantly. But here is the subtlety: saying "please keep this summary handy" does not itself build the summary — it just puts a sticky note saying "when you do build it, keep a copy." The summary is only actually built and kept the first time someone asks a question that needs it. That delayed behavior is why cache is lazy.
s1_definition.oneliner: Caching stores computed partitions on executors so later actions skip recomputation, and `cache()` is lazy because it only marks intent — the data is computed and stored on the first action that needs it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Caching in Spark keeps the computed partitions of an RDD or DataFrame in executor memory, and optionally on disk, so that subsequent actions reuse them instead of recomputing the whole lineage. The `cache()` method is lazy: calling it only marks the dataset to be cached and registers the intent with the storage system, but no computation and no storage happens until an action triggers execution, at which point the partitions are both computed and stored, and later actions read from the cache.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India spends an hour assembling a complicated summary of Rajesh's year of transactions. If every later question about that summary made him redo the whole hour of work, it would be madness. Caching is keeping that finished summary on his desk so the next ten questions are answered instantly. But here is the subtlety: saying "please keep this summary handy" does not itself build the summary — it just puts a sticky note saying "when you do build it, keep a copy." The summary is only actually built and kept the first time someone asks a question that needs it. That delayed behavior is why cache is lazy.

**One line to remember:** Caching stores computed partitions on executors so later actions skip recomputation, and `cache()` is lazy because it only marks intent — the data is computed and stored on the first action that needs it.

sections.s2_technical:
To understand caching you first need to remember that Spark transformations are lazy and every action re-triggers the entire lineage. So if you build a dataset through an expensive chain of filters, joins, and aggregations and then run several actions on it, Spark by default recomputes that whole chain from the source data for each action. Caching breaks this wasteful pattern: once a dataset is cached, the first action computes it and stores the resulting partitions on the executors, and every subsequent action reads those stored partitions directly, skipping the expensive recomputation.

The storage happens on the executors, distributed just like the data itself. Each executor holds the partitions it computed, in its memory by default, and the Driver keeps metadata about what is cached where. This is why caching helps most when a dataset is reused multiple times and is expensive to produce — iterative machine learning that passes over the same data, a dataset feeding several downstream branches, or interactive exploration where an analyst runs many queries on the same base.

Now the key question: why is cache lazy? Because cache does not change the fundamental rule that computation only happens on an action. Calling cache merely marks the dataset with a storage level and registers it with the block manager as "please persist my partitions when they are computed." No data is read and nothing is stored at that moment, exactly as with any transformation. The partitions are computed and cached only when the first action runs and actually forces the lineage to execute. This is consistent and deliberate: Spark never does work until an action demands a result, and cache is just a request that, when that work does happen, the output be kept.

A practical consequence follows from this laziness: the first action after caching is not faster — it does the full computation and additionally pays to store the result. The benefit appears from the second action onward, which reads the cache. Senior nuances include that cache is shorthand for persist with the default memory-and-disk storage level for DataFrames, that cached partitions can be evicted under memory pressure and transparently recomputed from lineage, that you must call unpersist to release the cache in long-running applications, and that sometimes people mistakenly expect cache to run eagerly or confuse it with collect, which actually pulls data to the Driver. In the bank, caching a cleaned, joined transaction dataset that fed five different daily reports turned five full recomputations into one computation plus five fast reads.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — An expensive cleaned dataset feeds several reports and is recomputed each time. This is exactly what caching avoids.

Problem 2 — People expect caching to speed up the very first run. This is exactly the misunderstanding that cache is lazy corrects.

Problem 3 — The cache must actually be built at the right moment and then reused. This is exactly the lazy-then-materialize behavior.

The mini-project models caching in Java. A `CachingDataset` has an expensive compute step with a counter, a cache flag set lazily by `cache()`, and action methods that either compute or read the cache. The demo builds an expensive aggregation of Rajesh's and Priya's transactions, calls cache, then runs three actions, showing that the first action materializes the cache and the next two reuse it, and that calling cache alone computed nothing.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the caching demo
java -cp target/caching-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.caching.CachingDemo

# Reference: real Spark
#   val cleaned = raw.filter(...).join(dim, "acct").groupBy("acct").sum("amount")
#   cleaned.cache()        // lazy — nothing happens yet
#   cleaned.count()        // ACTION → computes AND stores the cache
#   cleaned.show()         // reads from cache (no recompute)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: three transactions — Rajesh Rs.1000, Priya Rs.500, Rajesh Rs.3000 — feeding an expensive aggregation that we want to cache.

Step 1: The dataset is created and cache is called. This only sets a flag registering the intent to cache; the compute counter is still zero, proving that cache did no work. This is the laziness in action.

Step 2: The first action, counting accounts, runs. Because the cache is requested but not yet materialized, the expensive computation runs for the first time, producing totals of Rajesh Rs.4000 and Priya Rs.500. Since caching was requested, the result is stored, and the log notes the cache was materialized on this first action.

Step 3: The count returns two accounts. Note that this first action was not faster — it did the full computation and additionally paid to store the result, which is the expected consequence of lazy caching.

Step 4: The second action, the total for Rajesh, runs. The cache is now populated, so it reads the stored result directly and returns Rs.4000 without recomputing the aggregation.

Step 5: The third action, the total for Priya, also reads from the cache and returns Rs.500 with no recomputation.

Step 6: At the end, the expensive computation ran exactly once despite three actions, confirming that caching converted three full recomputations into one computation plus two fast cache reads, and that cache itself computed nothing until the first action.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] cache() called — intent registered ONLY (lazy, nothing computed/stored)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] after cache(): computeCount = 0 (still 0 → lazy!)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] EXPENSIVE compute run #1 (full lineage executed)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] cache MATERIALIZED on first action (computed + stored)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] accounts = 2
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] reading from CACHE (no recomputation)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] Rajesh total = 4000
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] reading from CACHE (no recomputation)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] Priya total = 500
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] total expensive computations = 1 (1, not 3 — caching worked)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  expensive dataset = filter → join → groupBy (costly)
    │
    ▼  cache()   ── LAZY: set flag only, computeCount=0 ──
  (nothing computed, nothing stored)
    │
    ▼  action #1: countAccounts()
  compute full lineage ONCE → {R:4000, P:500} → STORE in executor memory
    │
    ├── action #2: totalFor(R) → READ cache → 4000  (no recompute)
    └── action #3: totalFor(P) → READ cache → 500   (no recompute)
    │
    ▼
  expensive computations = 1 (for 3 actions)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Lazy Cache Mechanics ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Lazy Initialization: cache flag set now, value built later  │
  │     WHY: honor Spark's "work only on an action" rule         │
  │  Memoization: first action stores result; later reads reuse  │
  │     WHY: avoid recomputing an expensive lineage              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: CachingDataset models compute + cache + actions          │
  │  O: add a new action without changing cache logic            │
  │  D: actions depend on materialize(), not on compute directly │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           CachingDataset             │
  │──────────────────────────────────────│
  │ - source: List<Txn>                   │
  │ - cacheRequested: boolean (intent)    │
  │ - cached: Map (filled on 1st action)  │
  │ - computeCount: int                   │
  │──────────────────────────────────────│
  │ + cache(): CachingDataset  (LAZY)     │
  │ - expensiveCompute(): Map             │
  │ - materialize(): Map                  │
  │ + countAccounts(): long   (ACTION)    │
  │ + totalFor(acct): BigDecimal (ACTION) │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Cache ───────────────────────────────────────

  [UNCACHED] ──cache()──→ [MARKED(lazy)] ──1st action──→ [MATERIALIZED]
                                                  │ later actions
                                                  ▼
                                             [REUSED]
                              (eviction → recompute from lineage)

  ── Call Chain ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. CachingDemo.main()
  2.   → ds.cache()                 → flag only (computeCount 0)
  3.   → ds.countAccounts()         → compute #1 + store
  4.   → ds.totalFor("SAV2001")     → read cache
  5.   → ds.totalFor("CUR3001")     → read cache
  6.   → computeCount == 1
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Caching in Spark means keeping the computed partitions of an RDD or DataFrame on the executors, in memory by default and optionally on disk, so that subsequent actions reuse them instead of recomputing the entire lineage. It matters because Spark transformations are lazy and every action re-triggers the whole chain from the source, so if an expensive dataset built from filters, joins, and aggregations feeds several actions, Spark would recompute it fully each time. Caching breaks that: the first action computes and stores it, and every later action reads the stored partitions directly.

The reason cache is lazy is that it does not change Spark's fundamental rule that computation only happens on an action. Calling cache merely marks the dataset with a storage level and tells the block manager to persist its partitions when they are computed; it reads no data and stores nothing at that moment, exactly like any transformation. The partitions are actually computed and cached only when the first action forces the lineage to run. A direct consequence I always point out is that the first action after caching is not faster — it does the full computation and additionally pays to store the result — and the benefit only appears from the second action onward, which reads the cache.

In my project at the National Bank of India this was a routine, high-impact optimization. We had a cleaned, joined transaction dataset that fed about five different daily reports, and without caching Spark recomputed that expensive pipeline five times. Caching it turned that into one computation plus five fast reads, cutting the total runtime dramatically. The nuances I mention to show depth are that cache is shorthand for persist with a default storage level, that cached partitions can be evicted under memory pressure and are then transparently recomputed from lineage so caching is a performance optimization and not durable storage, that you must call unpersist to release the cache in long-running applications, and that people sometimes wrongly expect cache to run eagerly or confuse it with collect, which actually pulls data to the Driver.
